t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This is laboratory session no. 6. In it we examine the second distillate for chloroform, chloral hydrate and carbon tetrachloride, and learn to distinguish them from one another. The plan: differentiation of volatile chlorine-containing poisons. The aim is to study the reactions that distinguish toxicologically significant chlorine-containing substances in the distillate.

By the end of the session the student will be able to perform the reactions that differentiate chloroform, chloral hydrate and carbon tetrachloride. The work requires the distillate, flasks, test tubes, reagents, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

The group of alkyl halides includes chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride CCl4 and 1,2-dichloroethane. Distillation methods are used to isolate them from a biological object; chloroform and dichloroethane are steam-distilled. Remember: all compounds containing a chlorine atom give the reaction that converts organic chlorine into the chloride ion. This reaction is therefore common to the whole group.

Chloroform CHCl3 is a compound with a toxic effect on the body; it is used in industry, for stain removal, and in surgery as an anaesthetic. 5-10 g of chloroform leads to severe poisoning. Death results from paralysis of the respiratory centre, and the pathological findings are not characteristic. Chloroform is a colourless, clear liquid, heavier than water and poorly soluble in it, with a solubility of 1:200. It distils readily and rapidly with steam. In open air, under sunlight, it is oxidised to the highly toxic phosgene.

Let us consider chloroform poisoning and its elimination. 5-10 g of chloroform causes severe poisoning: severe stomach pain and nausea occur, and death results from paralysis of the respiratory centre. In chronic poisoning, liver function fails, cirrhosis of the liver develops, and the kidneys and heart muscle are damaged. Chloroform is eliminated from the body unchanged. The pathological findings are not characteristic.

In open air, under sunlight, chloroform is oxidised to form a highly toxic compound, namely phosgene. This process occurs in open air and in light. Chloroform evaporates in open air; it has a distinctive odour and a sweetish taste. It mixes well with ether and other organic solvents, and distils readily and rapidly with steam.

Chloral hydrate acts on the body in the same way as chloroform. In medicine it is used at about 0.2-0.5 g as a sedative and hypnotic preparation. It forms colourless crystals or a powder, readily soluble in water and ether. In an alkaline medium and at high temperature it decomposes to form chloroform. Carbon tetrachloride CCl4, in turn, rapidly damages the liver and kidneys and causes fatty degeneration of the liver; the medical dose is 3 ml. CCl4 and chloral hydrate are stored in cabinet B.

The dose and poisoning of chloral hydrate. It first stimulates the nervous system and then has a sedative effect. In medicine it is used at about 0.2-0.5 g as a hypnotic preparation. In poisoning, an adverse effect on the cardiovascular system, rapid breathing, a fall in body temperature and constriction of the pupils are observed. Death results from cessation of breathing and heartbeat. Chloral hydrate is stored in cabinet B.

t: Decomposition of chloral hydrate in alkali
n: Chloral hydrate forms colourless, clear crystals or a powder with a pungent odour and a bitter taste; it is readily soluble in water and ether. In an alkaline medium and at high temperature it decomposes to form chloroform. This is decomposition by alkali on heating. An important property: because chloral hydrate is a crystalline substance, it does not evaporate together with ether at room temperature. The distinction between chloroform and chloral hydrate is based precisely on this.

CCl4 is used to dissolve varnishes, oil paints and rubber, to preserve skin and wool, as an anthelmintic, and in fire extinguishing. In poisoning, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness and dizziness are observed. The liver and kidneys are rapidly damaged, jaundice develops, and fatty degeneration of the liver occurs. CCl4 is rapidly absorbed through mucous membranes. When used as a medicine, fatty food must be avoided; the dose is 3 ml. It is stored in cabinet B, and staff undergo a medical examination every 6 months.

1,2-Dichloroethane, DCE for short, differs from chloroform and CCl4 in that it burns with a smoky flame. In DCE poisoning, vomiting, diarrhoea, pain in the liver, abdominal distension and uraemia are observed. 15-20 ml of DCE is fatal. DCE is isolated from the biological object by steam distillation. Remember: analysis of dichloroethane in the distillate, in accordance with the special manual, is performed only on the instructor's directions.

t: Step 1: converting organic chlorine to chloride ion
n: In the first step, organic chlorine is converted into the chloride ion. To 1-2 ml of distillate, 1 ml of 10% alcoholic NaOH solution is added, and the mixture is boiled for 2-3 minutes on a water bath. After cooling, it is acidified with 10% HNO3 and 0.5 ml of 5% AgNO3 is added. A white precipitate or turbidity forms. In another test tube, the reaction is carried out under the same conditions with purified water, and the results are compared.

We now turn to the interpretation of the first reaction. If the precipitate or turbidity dissolves in 25% ammonia solution, this indicates halogen derivatives in the distillate. All compounds containing a chlorine atom give this reaction. For this reason the reaction has negative forensic chemical significance. Thus this reaction does not distinguish between the substances: it is positive for chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4.

t: Equations of the chloride ion reaction
n: The equations of the chloride ion reaction. When chloroform is heated with alcoholic alkali, formic acid and NaCl are formed. After cooling, in a nitric acid medium, AgNO3 gives a white precipitate. All compounds containing a chlorine atom, for example CCl4, give this reaction. The reaction therefore has negative forensic chemical significance: it does not distinguish between the substances.

The isonitrile reaction. To 1 ml of the second distillate, 10 drops of 10% sodium hydroxide in alcohol and one drop of aniline are added, and the mixture is heated for 1-2 minutes. The appearance of a foul odour indicates the formation of isonitrile. The reaction is performed in a fume cupboard. Then a small amount of sulphuric acid is added to the test tube: the isonitrile is hydrolysed, the foul odour is eliminated, and the mixture is poured away. The reaction is given by CCl4 and chloral hydrate; dichloroethane does not give it.

The essence of the isonitrile reaction: if aniline and alkali are added to the distillate and the mixture is heated, isonitrile with a characteristic foul odour is formed. This reaction is given by CCl4 and chloral hydrate; dichloroethane does not give it. The reaction is performed in a fume cupboard. The foul odour is eliminated with sulphuric acid.

The resorcinol and Fehling reactions. In the resorcinol reaction, 1 ml of freshly prepared 1% resorcinol in alkali is added to 1 ml of distillate. The mixture is heated on a boiling water bath for 2-10 minutes, and a violet or red colour appears. As a control, 1 ml of purified water is taken in another test tube; its colour must not change. In the Fehling reaction, 2 ml of distillate is heated with 2 ml of Fehling's solutions 1 and 2 over a gas flame for 5-10 minutes. First yellow copper(II) hydroxide, then red copper(I) oxide precipitates.

The Fujiwara reaction. When pyridine is heated with alkyl halides in an alkaline medium on a water bath, a red colour forms. A pyridine salt is formed, which in the alkaline medium passes into glutaconic aldehyde derivatives. As a result, a red colour appears. The Fujiwara reaction is one of the reactions characteristic of dichloroethane.

The second distillate is collected in a volume of 25 ml into an empty clean flask, using steam distillation. The second distillate is used to detect alcohols, aldehydes and ketones, alkyl halides, aromatic hydrocarbon derivatives and other substances. To distinguish chloroform from chloral hydrate, an ether extract is prepared from the distillate in pure form.

t: Chemical basis of the Fehling reaction
n: The chemical basis of the Fehling reaction is as follows. In the presence of alkali, chloroform forms formic acid. Formic acid reduces copper(II) hydroxide: first yellow CuOH, then red Cu2O precipitates. This reaction is given by substances with reducing properties: CHCl3, chloral hydrate and formaldehyde. CCl4 and dichloroethane do not give it. The sequence of equations: CHCl3 + 3NaOH → HCOOH + NaCl + H2O, then CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4.

t: Algorithm for differentiating chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4
n: The algorithm for differentiating chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4. First we convert organic chlorine into the chloride ion: all organochlorine compounds give a positive result, that is, this step does not differentiate. Then the Fehling reaction is performed: it is given by chloroform and chloral hydrate, not by CCl4. If it is positive, the sample is shaken with ether and the ether is evaporated; if the reaction in the residue is positive, it is chloral hydrate, if negative, chloroform.

Documenting and interpreting the result. In the chemical part of the report, the methods, reactions, reagents and apparatus are recorded in order on the basis of the laboratory notebook. In this part of the report it is forbidden to write chemical formulae or to cite the name of any author. When a substance is detected, quantitative analysis must always be performed, because in some cases reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may be obtained.

Let us summarise the reaction results. Conversion of organic chlorine to Cl- is positive for chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4. The isonitrile reaction is given by chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4. The Fehling reaction is given by chloroform and chloral hydrate, but not by CCl4. Resorcinol gives a violet or red colour if chloroform, chloral hydrate or CCl4 is present. Thus, only the Fehling reaction in the table sets CCl4 apart.

The procedure for distinguishing chloroform from chloral hydrate. 10 ml of distillate is shaken 2-3 times with 5 ml of ether, and the ether is filtered into a dry vessel. The ether is evaporated at room temperature, and the residue is dissolved in 1-2 ml of water and tested. A positive result indicates chloral hydrate, because it does not evaporate with ether. A negative result indicates chloroform, because it evaporates.

t: Distinguishing chloroform and chloral hydrate from CCl4
n: We distinguish chloroform and chloral hydrate from CCl4. Chloroform and chloral hydrate are able to reduce copper(II) hydroxide, whereas carbon tetrachloride does not give this reaction. The "Wheel" table also lists the Fujiwara reaction and the reactions with 2,7-dihydroxynaphthalene and with Nessler's reagent. Analysis of dichloroethane in the distillate, in accordance with the special manual, is performed only on the instructor's directions.

Characteristic reactions of dichloroethane. When DCE is heated with alkali, the chlorine atom is not released completely, so detection by the ordinary chloride reaction is limited. In the copper acetylide reaction, if 1,2-dichloroethane and NaOH are boiled in an ampoule, acetylene is formed. With copper salts it gives copper acetylide, pink or cherry red. DCE does not form isonitrile and does not react with Fehling's solution.

Distinguishing dichloroethane from the others. 1,2-Dichloroethane differs from chloroform and CCl4 in that it burns with a smoky flame. DCE does not form isonitrile, does not react with Fehling's solution or resorcinol, and its chlorine is not released completely in alkali. It is characterised by the Fujiwara reaction, the copper acetylide reaction, and the reaction forming formaldehyde from ethylene glycol.

The copper acetylide reaction of DCE. If 1,2-dichloroethane and NaOH are placed in an ampoule, sealed, and boiled on a water bath, acetylene is formed. With copper salts, acetylene forms copper acetylide, pink or cherry red. Remember: this reaction is performed only on the instructor's directions.

Another route of DCE analysis passes through ethylene glycol to formaldehyde. Nazarenko and Lapkina showed in 1952 that chlorine is readily released from DCE on heating under pressure in a sealed ampoule, in the presence of bicarbonate or in an alkaline medium. The ethylene glycol formed is oxidised to formaldehyde and detected with chromotropic acid or fuchsin-sulphurous acid. In the presence of mineral acids, formaldehyde gives a pink colour.

The amount of alkyl halides is determined by the argentometric method after the organically bound chlorine has been released; the indicator is ferric ammonium alum. The amount of dichloroethane is likewise determined by the argentometric method after the organic chlorine has been released. The review questions ask about the analysis of alkyl halides by GLC and their quantification.

Case 5: poisoning with a fire extinguisher agent. A blood sample from a person poisoned by the contents of one of the fire extinguishers was brought to forensic chemical examination for analysis; the poisoning was caused by a chemical substance. Question: for which substance do the initial assumptions indicate that analysis should be carried out? Justify the solution with specific facts. Recall: CCl4 is used in medicine and veterinary practice, and in fire extinguishing. Its heavy vapour extinguishes burning oil and petrol by cutting them off from atmospheric oxygen.

The solution pathway for case 5. The case presents a blood sample from a person poisoned by the contents of one of the fire extinguishers; the poisoning was caused by a chemical substance. CCl4 is used in the extinguishing agent, and this is the working assumption. The second distillate is then obtained by steam distillation. If organic chlorine is converted into Cl-, all alkyl halides give a positive result. In the Fehling reaction CCl4 is negative, while chloroform and chloral hydrate are positive. The amount is determined by argentometry or GLC.

t: Situational problem 1: yellowed liver and kidneys
n: Situational problem 1. The internal organs of the corpse of "S.F.", born in 1961, were submitted: liver, stomach and kidneys. Portions of the liver and kidneys are yellowed and covered with fat. In the preliminary analysis, the second distillate was boiled with alcoholic NaOH, acidified with HNO3, and 0.5 ml of 5% AgNO3 was added; a white precipitate formed that dissolves in 25% ammonia. Question: for which toxic substances are the forensic chemical analyses to be carried out?

Situational problem 2. The internal organs of the corpse of "U.L.", born in 1972, were submitted: liver, stomach and oesophagus. Portions of the stomach and oesophagus have a distinctive smell of chlorine. In the preliminary analysis, when 2 ml of distillate was heated with 2 ml of Fehling's solutions 1 and 2 for 5-10 minutes, yellow copper(II) hydroxide and then red copper(I) oxide precipitated. Question: for which toxic substances are the forensic chemical analyses to be carried out?

Let us consider the line of reasoning in the situational problems. In problem 1 the liver and kidneys are yellowed and fatty; in the second distillate the Cl- reaction is positive, that is, a white precipitate soluble in ammonia. In problem 2 there is a smell of chlorine in the stomach and oesophagus, and the Fehling reaction is positive: a yellow, then red precipitate. CCl4 rapidly damages the liver and kidneys and causes fatty degeneration of the liver. With Fehling's reagent, however, it is chloroform and chloral hydrate that react.

Reactions in the "Wheel" table: detection of organic chlorine, isonitrile, resorcinol, Fehling I and II, Fujiwara, 2,7-dihydroxynaphthalene and Nessler's reagent. The substances to be tested: chloroform, chloral hydrate and CCl4. Exercise: for each substance choose the appropriate reactions and record the change observed.

The review questions are as follows. Which substances belong to the alkyl halides, what is their toxicological and narcological significance, and what are the signs of poisoning and the metabolism? What are the conditions for converting organically bound chlorine into the inorganic chloride ion, and which organochlorine compounds form isonitrile? How do chloroform and chloral hydrate react with Fehling's solution, and why does CCl4 not react with Fehling's reagent? What is the distinguishing feature of chloroform and chloral hydrate, how is CCl4 detected in the distillate, and can they be analysed by GLC?

Safety and conclusion. The isonitrile reaction is performed in a fume cupboard, and the foul odour is eliminated with sulphuric acid. Under light, chloroform is oxidised to the highly toxic phosgene; CCl4 and chloral hydrate are stored in cabinet B. The differentiation procedure: the Cl- reaction is given by all of them, Fehling's reaction sets CCl4 apart, and evaporation with ether separates chloroform from chloral hydrate.
